51423416.DESCRIPTION: Binding affinity to TTR V30M mutant (unknown origin) by isothermal titration calorimetry

original_paragraph.ITC Measurements: In order to reduce the concentration of DMSO during the ITC experiment, a reverse ITC experiment, in which compound solution was titrated with a protein solution, was adopted. Prior to the ITC experiment, the buffer of V30M-TTR was exchanged with ITC buffer (50 mM NaPi pH 7.5, 50 mM NaCl, and DMSO) by repetition of dilution and concentration. The protein concentration was adjusted to 300–600 μM for the titrant solution. The concentrations of 1, 2, 3, and 42 for the cell solutions were 30, 30, 60, and 60 μM, respectively. ITC measurements were carried out at 298 K with a MicroCal iTC200 microcalorimeter (Malvern Instruments, Malvern, UK), using 750 rpm stirring and 180 s delay between injections to the sample cell. The first injection (0.8 μL) was followed by 18 injections of 2 μL. Thermogram peaks were integrated using NITPIC followed by a curve fitting to a single binding-site model using SEDPHAT. The figures of the representative thermogram and binding isotherm were prepared using GUSI (University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX).
original_paragraph.Figure 5 caption: Figure 5. (a) Representative thermograms and isothermal titration curves for the binding of 42 (a), 3 (b), 1 (c), and 2 (d) to V30M-TTR.
original_paragraph.Thermodynamic Analysis of the Binding of: The ANS-competitive binding and the methanol-induced aggregation assays suggested that 42 binds to the T4-binding site of TTR with high affinity. The thermodynamic parameters of the binding of 42 to V30M-TTR were characterized using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). All ITC isotherms exhibited obvious uniphasic structures, and uniphasic ITC data are generally not well-suited to the refinement of multiple thermodynamic parameters (Figure 5). The ITC curves were fitted to the model with two identical and independent binding sites because fitting to the model with the sequential binding sites gave the worse statistical parameters. The dissociation constant (Kd) for 42 was 0.062 μM. The Kd value for 42 was comparable with that for 3 and significantly lower than those for 1 (p < 0.05) and 2 (p < 0.001), indicating that 42 more tightly binds to V30M-TTR than the clinical drugs (Table 3). The Kd value for 1 with WT-TTR was 0.2 μM, while the Kd value of the first site for 1 with WT-TTR was previously shown to be in the nanomolar range. The structurally unstable V30M-TTR may exhibit lowered affinity with 1. The bindings of 2 and 3 were enthalpy-driven, and the enthalpy and entropy changes contributed to the binding of 1. These results are consistent with the previous studies. In the binding of 42, the enthalpy and entropy changes equally contributed to the Gibbs free energy change, showing a thermodynamic signature similar to that of 1. Favorable entropy changes generally originate from the desolvation entropy. The binding of 42 with the hydrophobic chloride groups is likely to induce the effective release of water molecules from the binding sites, resulting in the favorable binding entropy. The previous ITC studies using WT-TTR have shown that the Kd value of 3 is higher than that of 2. In contrast, our ITC experiments using V30M-TTR revealed that the Kd value of 3 was lower than that of 2, corresponding to the results of the ANS-competitive binding assay. Structural comparison of WT-TTR–1 (PDB 3TCT) and V30M-TTR–1 (PDB 6E72) revealed that the binding modes of 1 in WT-TTR and V30M-TTR were quite similar (Supporting Information Figure S3). Although the comparison is necessarily limited due to the lack of the crystal structure of the V30M-TTR–3 complex, the V30M-TTR proteins with structural fluctuations may prefer 3 with a dominant contribution from enthalpy to 2 with equal contributions from enthalpy and entropy.
